Okay. So, you brought us an architecture diagram of the bank in a box project. What is bank in a box?
Bank in a box is, let me go a step back. Bank in a box is because we have the Avalok ecosystem.

Sure. Sure. The first thing that we need to think is when you want to automate something, you need to have a core, you need to have a brain.
So, on one side we have the users that actually request something from your automation.
And your automation here, we target EKS because here we build all the service that we need to automate all the infrastructure.

Mm-hmm. Okay.
So, now our idea was to say, okay, when a customer or a partner or a fintech request for an account with us, we said, we map it directly to the account that we have in Amazon.
So, the customer requests for an account, we spin up an account for the customer, and when that account is ready, then we're ready to provision the sandbox.
And the sandbox.

Everything is based on EC2 instances, and we leverage through the AMIs.
So, and the customer, when he sends it, so after the account is being created, EKS, even the different services, pull everything together and start spinning up like the ABS.

Wow.

They need to provision like the whole infrastructure, install the software, and that's why we use immutable infrastructure to speed up the process.
Furthermore, also for the accounts, we pre-bake the account.
So, we use organization, organizational unit, so that we prepare already accounts, so warm accounts.

Why EKS?

You're interested about the worker nodes because you have your services that you want to deploy on Kubernetes.
So, and we didn't want to take care about the whole control plane because it can get a mess.
I mean, you need to take care of it, you need to make sure that it's updated and so forth.
But by using EKS, we are just concerned about running the images.
So, use the Kubernetes APIs to deploy our stuff.
